title: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Salary: CFO Salary Insights and Casual Loading
description: Learn to convert hourly pay to annual salary using 38-hour weeks, casual loading, and super. Includes CFO salary context, tax estimates, and Fair Work rates.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super. For example, at the national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour, annual gross is $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44. If you receive casual loading of 25%, your hourly rate becomes $33.05, and annual gross becomes $65,306.80.

faqs.q: Does casual loading affect my superannuation?
faqs.a: Yes. Superannuation is calculated on your ordinary time earnings, which includes casual loading. So if your casual rate is $33.05 per hour (including 25% loading), your employer pays 12% super on top of that – an extra $3.966 per hour. The super guarantee is paid on top of your gross pay, not deducted from it, and is capped at the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the national minimum wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The national minimum wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is the legal minimum for award/agreement-free employees. Award rates are higher minimums set by industry or occupation awards, which often include penalty rates, allowances, and higher base pay. Most employees are covered by an award, so you should check the relevant pay guide from the Fair Work Ombudsman to see your correct minimum rate.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Hourly to Annual: The Basics

If you’re paid by the hour and want to know your annual salary, the standard formula is simple: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52**. This assumes you work the same number of hours every week of the year, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For full-time employees, the standard week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Commission. That means annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52.

For example, a casual worker on the national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour (before loading) would earn $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44 per year. If you’re paid fortnightly, your gross fortnight pay is your weekly pay multiplied by two. So weekly pay of $1,004.90 becomes $2,009.80 per fortnight.

This conversion is the starting point for understanding your total remuneration, including superannuation and tax. The [timesheet](/) on this site lets you enter your base hourly rate and toggle casual loading to see the annual figures instantly.

## National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The **national minimum wage** from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours, according to the Fair Work Commission. This is the minimum for adult employees not covered by an award or agreement. For casual employees, a 25% loading applies, making the casual rate $33.05 per hour ($1,256.13 per week).

However, most employees are covered by an award – a legal document that sets minimum pay rates, penalties, and allowances for a specific industry or occupation. Award rates are almost always higher than the national minimum wage. You can find the correct rate for your job using the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman. These guides list minimum pay for full-time, part-time, and casual employees, and include the most common penalty rates and allowances.

If you’re a CFO or senior executive, your salary is likely well above award rates. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings were $2,083.70 in May 2026. A **cfo salary** in Australia often exceeds $200,000 per year, but the same hourly-to-annual conversion applies if you’re paid an hourly rate or a salary expressed per hour.

## Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for the lack of paid leave (annual leave, sick leave) and other entitlements. It is not included in the base rate – you add it on top. When using the [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) calculator, always enter your base hourly rate first, then tick the casual loading box to see the loaded rate.

Superannuation is paid on top of your gross pay. The super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, which includes casual loading if you’re a casual employee. So if your casual rate is $33.05 per hour, your employer pays an additional $3.966 per hour into your super fund. Super is capped at the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year – once your ordinary earnings exceed that, no further super is required.

For a CFO earning a high salary, super is still paid on the first $270,830 of earnings. Salary packaging arrangements (such as sacrificing part of your salary into super or a car) can affect the taxable amount, but the calculator on this site assumes no salary sacrifice.

## Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your annual gross pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies marginal tax rates for residents in 2026–27:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (the single reduction thresholds used here are from 2025–26 as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool on this site estimates your net annual pay after tax and Medicare, but does not deduct HELP loans, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

For example, a casual worker earning $65,306.80 per year (at $33.05 per hour) would pay approximately $10,546 in tax plus $1,306 in Medicare levy, leaving a take-home of about $53,455. Their super would be $7,836.82 paid on top.

## Putting It All Together

Whether you’re checking the national minimum wage, comparing a job offer, or estimating a **cfo salary**, the same principles apply: start with your hourly rate, multiply by hours per week and 52 weeks, add casual loading if applicable, then add super on top. Use the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) reference for base rates, and the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) data from the ABS for context.

Remember that this is an estimate. Your actual pay may differ due to overtime, penalty rates, allowances, enterprise agreements, or salary packaging. Always check your award or agreement for the exact rules.
